chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abdullah ibn Ahmad al-Razi, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah al-Basri, who said:

I was present when Ibn Abi Layla judged in the case of a man who had assigned the usufruct (income/produce) of a house to some of his relatives but did not specify a time limit for them. The man died, so his heirs came to Ibn Abi Layla, and the heirs of the person to whom the house was assigned also came. Ibn Abi Layla said: 'I think I should leave it (the house/usufruct) in the state in which its owner left it.'
Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Thaqafi said to him: 'Indeed, Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) judged in this mosque contrary to what you have judged.'

He said: 'And what is your knowledge?' He said: 'I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) judged with the return of the usufruct and the execution of the inheritances.'

Ibn Abi Layla said: 'Is it with you in a book?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Send for it and bring it to me.' Muhammad ibn Muslim said: 'On the condition that you do not look in the book except for that hadith.' He said: 'That is agreed.'
So he showed him the hadith from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) in the book, and he reversed his judgment.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.الْحَبِيسُ: The usufruct or produce held in reserve/attached
key_terms.غَلَّةَ دَارٍ: Usufruct or income/produce of a house

ai.seo_question: How did the judges determine the status of a house with an indefinite usufruct grant upon the owner's death?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the transmission of judicial precedent from the Ahl al-Bayt to early jurists, specifically highlighting how Muhammad ibn Muslim invoked the ruling of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) regarding the return of usufruct (*habis*) to ensure the full execution of inheritance (*mawarith*). The narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the continuity of legal authority from the Imams, demonstrating that even established judges like Ibn Abi Layla were subject to correction based on the precise teachings of the Imams. It serves as a key example of how specific rulings on property rights were preserved and applied in practical legal disputes during the early Islamic period.
